Land Reform - Expropriation: The Final Act

By: ALTYDVRYSTAAT PRODUCTIONS | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Emotions recently ran high at a meeting between Police Minister Bheki Cele, farmers, and farm dwellers in Normandien in northern KwaZulu-Natal. Cele met with the farming community over concerns about

Unique Selling Point:
Farmers of all class, race and economic status claim the Dept of Land Reform is driving a wedge between South Africans in rural KZN with the tenure claim system that is not working, leaving residents with more questions than answers.

Summary:
Farmers in KZN blame the department of land reform for the friction in the region. According to farmers of different races, specifically the tenure claimants are a thorn in their flesh. They also lay the spate of stock thefts and farm arson in the area at the door of these claimants. Poor policing and lack of police resources also feature. A person living on a farm can for instance claim tenancy if they can prove their family has lived on that land for longer than a certain amount of time. Yet farmers say, the department requires very little proof before they register a claim. There is also a massive disconnect between the department and SAPS with SAPS “often claiming they can’t arrest.” Ex-rugby player Anton Pitout (43) has tried to register more than ten cases against the Macu-family living on his farm Elandsklip (in the Normandien-area of Northern KZN). “I have tried opening cases for assault, intimidation and contempt of court. SAPS find a different excuse to not register the cases every time.” Of these cases, only one (for assault) is presently open. In one such case, Pitout claims he was assaulted by the Macu-family. He took a video of part of the assault. When he approached his local police, he was told they couldn’t open the case because he couldn’t prove it was him taking the video. Pitout spent R140 000 last year in order to get an interdict to stop the Macu-family chasing their goats into his crops. Since then nothing has changed. Sipho Hadebe (72) bought his farm in the same area with no government assistance. Hadebe says farmers of all races work together, but the tenant claimants and politicians “from outside” make things difficult. “Corruption has eaten all the money. Now they are coming for the farms. This government will turn Normandien into Somalia.”Abu Docrat (32) claims a local politician built a house on a part of his land and gave it to the care taker of a local school. Docrat farms cattle and sheep on just over a 1000 hectares in Normandien

Further information:
Case Studies:

Pitout (Afrikaans).

Experts:

KZN Land Reform: Visual Treatment
The new Land Expropriation Bill was gazetted on 9 October 2020, coupled with
tensions running high about farm attacks and the lack of consistent law
enforcement in our rural areas… a recipe for fear and frustration…
Prof Elmien du Plessis is an expert on constitutional law and land expropriation.
We meet her in a library/study setting. She will be filmed without the presenter,
with 2x cameras (one sideview). She explains the new bill and the implications
thereof. Link & Drone driving shots take us to KZN...
The bulk of the insert will be filmed in the Normandien and Newcastle region of
northern KZN. Expansive drone shots and extreme wide establishers will reveal
the lush landscape to be juxtaposed against the close-ups of the destruction on
the farmers’ land. Pitout’s farm shows damage from the grazing cattle and 50+
goats. Huts on the Ameen farm have been burnt down. There is also cell-phone
footage of an attack on Pitout, and intimidation from the farm occupiers.
The interviews with the three farmers will be filmed outside (weather permitting)
in a casual stance overlooking their property, or whilst working on the farm. The
plan is to let the presenter assist, hands-on, while they are doing the interview.
We’re going into planting season for maize, so fields need to be ploughed etc…
Pitout has a maize farm, the others have livestock incl. cattle and sheep. We will
try and capture the textures of the land, with close-ups of soil, livestock, crops
and whatever else we find.

Script:


LAND REFORM SCRIPT

V/O Our constitution makes provision for equitable redistribution of resources in South Africa, and one of these is Land… But Land reform has never been straightforward and countrywide people are getting impatient….
LINK The Expropriation Bill was Gazetted on the 9th of October, paving the way for expropriation of land without compensation…. Understandably making landowners anxious.
Elmien du Plessis Expropriation in the bigger scheme of land reform is only a method for the state to acquire the property.
V/O Prof Elmien du Plessis from the Law Faculty at the University of the North-West, lectures land reform, indigenous and property law. She says the new bill is simply a document that sets out processes to follow if, and when, a piece of land will be expropriated as part of the Land reform process.
Elmien du Plessis Our constitution contains mainly three programmes for land reform. The one is land redistribution. We want to redistribute land to for instance black farmers who can farm the land. We also have a land restitution program where you could claim to put in a claim for land if your land was taken away from you and to comply with the requirements
V/O The third, and probably more challenging of the programmes is land tenure.. This deals with farm dwellers and tenants who are situated on land, in some cases for generations, but do not have ownership and do not necessarily work there. In the embattled Normandien region of KZN tensions are running high in the daily land rights tug-of-war.
Elmien du Plessis How do you balance the rights that the farmer has with. you know, the rights that the farm dwellers or the labour tenants in many instances had lost and and and and the way that their lives have been reduced to an agreement that tells them that they must limit the number of cattle they keep.

V/O Livestock numbers is one of the primary points of conflict here, and Du Plessis says the duty of the farmers - preserving the agricultural land - and the farm dwellers’ dream of escaping the poverty cycle by investing in more livestock, is putting them at odds with each other
Lucky Shabalala There is nothing I can do with five livestock, I cannot take my child to university with five livestock. I cannot buy food for myself with five livestock.
V/O Lucky Shabalala, a self proclaimed community leader and land activist, is frustrated with how the process is playing out.
Lucky Shabalala It is not like we keep our livestock to just look at them and see, oh they are growing. We keep our livestock to do business, but it is just that we are excluded from the economic development by the government and those who are owning the land.
V/O He believes the system is unfairly balanced in favour of the land owners.
Lucky Shabalala You see, they are having more than five hundred livestock or a thousand livestock, in a farm. In one farm, but they want us to have five livestock. It’s unfair. We want to be commercial farmers like them.
Elmien du Plessis The interesting thing of labour tenants of course is that these are people in most instances who can already farm, they have done so for centuries and if you look far back in the history around nineteen hundreds these their forefathers were often very successful black commercial farmers.
LINK From an agricultural view, this is fertile soil, ripe for planting, but it has become the symbol that represents the divide between the haves and the have-nots.
V/O Anton Pitout, a retired provincial rugby player and Sevens Springbok, bought his first farm in 2018. Together with the title deed, he received a signed occupancy agreement between the previous owner and the Macu’s, a family with tenure on his farm. Almost immediately the battle lines were drawn.
Anton Pitout Die mense wat daar bly het het net geweier om om 'n dier uit die lande te hou. Hulle het geweier om die kampe te gebruik. Hulle het die diere het die hele plaas vol geloop. Jy kan nie met hulle praat nie hulle praat nie, hulle raak aggressief. Ons begin baklei.
V/O Over the last two years several heated confrontations between Pitout and the Macu’s followed, resulting in an assault charge and a charge of intimidation (both against members of the Macu-family) being laid.
Anton Pitout Ek moet op my regte staan ek moet my eiendom beskerm ek moet in die einde van die maand moet ek die banke terug betaal vir daai plaas en en hulle verstaan dit nie.
V/O At the heart of the conflict between Pitout and the Macu’s is a dispute about the true ownership of the land. Ahe Macu-family believes Pitout stole the land even though he has a title deed for the farm, known as Elandsklip.
Lucky Shabalala No the guy doesn’t own the farm. He doesn’t have papers that proves that he owns the farm.

V/O We spoke to the Macu-family but they did not want to be interviewed on camera. However, Shabalala claims to be well acquainted with their story.
Lucky Shabalala He just ploughed where the cattle of the Macu family were grazing. By force and that is where the fight started because the people said to him but you cannot plough here because our livestock are grazing here. He said but the farm belongs to me, there is nothing that you can do to me.
V/O When mielie-season is over it might not be a huge problem, but when the Macu goats start eating the profits, it spells trouble.
V/O Pitout maintains he did more that was required of him to accommodate the Macu’s. He fenced off 90ha of his farm for their livestock and sank a borehole for them.
Anton Pitout Hulle is nie tevrede nie. Hulle wil van my ontslae raak. Hulle wil my van die plaas af hê sodat hulle kan oorneem hierso.
V/O The Macu’s see it differently. They say the portion of land that they have access to is unproductive and they claim the borehole doesn’t work properly.

Desperate for relief, Pitout approached the land claims court in Roodepoort. At a cost of R140 000 he was awarded an interdict, but he feels it was money wasted …
Anton Pitout Land Affairs wil nie betrokke raak nie. Jy staan alleen en ek dis absoluut onregverdig en dan word jy geoormerk as rassis en hierdie verskriklike monster.
LINK In South Africa, any conversation around land reform is an emotive one. One the one hand people need land, on the other there are existing landowners. Both have rights but finding a win-win solution is proving to be difficult.
V/O Even the low hanging fruit of the “willing buyer, willing seller’ concept seems to be having its own problems.
Elmien du Plessis The problem with a willing buyer willing seller is when the land was validated either it was not evaluated correctly by the land valuers because farmland for instance got a very specific way of valuing and then oftentimes offers were made to owners that were just so good to refuse.
V/O A lot of government money was spent on purchasing land..
Elmien du Plessis Some of the land owners inflated the prices exponentially. I wouldn't say in the whole it didn't work. I still think it's a good way of acquiring land if there's cooperation.
V/O Newcastle farmers Darrel Brown and Sam Nkosi, started off on the wrong foot in 1996 when Brown bought the farm where Nkosi’s family has been living since 1968. After years of disputes over land rights, something changed...
Sam Nkosi I took my my own pride, I said that I’d rather sit down with Mr. Brown to tell him, “What are we fighting for? That was my biggest question. We're fighting for what?
Darrel Brown When Sam and I actually started talking I agreed to cut off a piece of the farm to sell to government to sort out the problem ..
V/O But this turned out to be easier said than done...
Darrel Brown The frustration that we've faced is we've had no support from the Department of Land Affairs in getting the matter finalized.
Sam Nkosi The government has promised us more than about seven years now waiting for the next budget that the farm should be bought. But we’re waiting for that budget for I don’t know how long now, more than seven years.
V/O For Brown it is also important that Nkosi gets a formal title deed for the land once the deal is formalised.
Darrel Brown Well I think everybody. Wants to feel proud 01:45 of the fact that they own something. It would give him a sense of self actualization to give him a sense of what he's achieving something and he's able and privileged to then go ahead and farm it productively and hopefully use it as a stepping stone to buy something bigger and become a proper commercial farmer.

V/O In the meantime, for Brown the dark cloud of expropriation without compensation hovers on the horizon.
Darrel Brown We've spent a lot of money on that land and whilst we may be willing to to sell pieces of that land or some of that land in the interests of land reform I don't think any of us want to give up our hard earned land for nothing.
Elmien Du Plessis We must remember that the Constitution provides the framework so it must still be just and equitable. So if it's not just and equitable to pay nil the state will not be able to do it...
V/O Du Plessis says the bill sets out examples of the types of land that could potentially be expropriated without compensation, for example abandoned or unused land.
Elmien du Plessis I think what they tried to do is to just give an indication of the type of land that they have in mind just to ensure people that they don't have in mind to take big commercial working farms and to dump us into a food security crisis.

PROMO 1 11” Land Reform is a complex issue, and balancing the needs of the landless with the rights of landowners is proving to be a challenge. Will the new expropriation bill be the magic bullet?
PROMO 2 11” The new expropriation bill paves the way for expropriation without compensation but will it make a meaningful difference to our sluggish land reform process?
PROMO 3 11” Farm dwellers with historic rights to land vs title deed owners. The precarious balancing act of Land Reform continues to be a frustration for many South Africans.

This deals with farm dwellers and tenants who are situated on land, in some cases for generations, but do not have ownership and do not necessarily work there. Elmien du Plessis How do you balance the rights that the farmer has with. you know, the rights that the farm dwellers or the labour tenants in many instances had lost and and and and the way that their lives have been reduced to an agreement that tells them that they must limit the number of cattle they keep. V/O Livestock numbers is one of the primary points of conflict here, and Du Plessis says the duty of the farmers - preserving the agricultural land - and the farm dwellers’ dream of escaping the poverty cycle by investing in more livestock, is putting them at odds with each other Lucky Shabalala There is nothing I can do with five livestock, I cannot take my child to university with five livestock. I cannot buy food for myself with five livestock. V/O Lucky Shabalala, a self proclaimed community leader and land activist, is frustrated with how the process is playing out. Lucky Shabalala It is not like we keep our livestock to just look at them and see, oh they are growing. We keep our livestock to do business, but it is just that we are excluded from the economic development by the government and those who are owning the land. V/O He believes the system is unfairly balanced in favour of the land owners. Lucky Shabalala You see, they are having more than five hundred livestock or a thousand livestock, in a farm. In one farm, but they want us to have five livestock. It’s unfair. We want to be commercial farmers like them. Elmien du Plessis The interesting thing of labour tenants of course is that these are people in most instances who can already farm, they have done so for centuries and if you look far back in the history around nineteen hundreds these their forefathers were often very successful black commercial farmers. LINK From an agricultural view, this is fertile soil, ripe for planting, but it has become the symbol that represents the divide between the haves and the have-nots. V/O Anton Pitout, a retired provincial rugby player and Sevens Springbok, bought his first farm in 2018. Together with the title deed, he received a signed occupancy agreement between the previous owner and the Macu’s, a family with tenure on his farm. Almost immediately the battle lines were drawn. Anton Pitout Die mense wat daar bly het het net geweier om om 'n dier uit die lande te hou. Hulle het geweier om die kampe te gebruik. Hulle het die diere het die hele plaas vol geloop. Jy kan nie met hulle praat nie hulle praat nie, hulle raak aggressief. Ons begin baklei. V/O Over the last two years several heated confrontations between Pitout and the Macu’s followed, resulting in an assault charge and a charge of intimidation (both against members of the Macu-family) being laid. Anton Pitout Ek moet op my regte staan ek moet my eiendom beskerm ek moet in die einde van die maand moet ek die banke terug betaal vir daai plaas en en hulle verstaan dit nie. V/O At the heart of the conflict between Pitout and the Macu’s is a dispute about the true ownership of the land. Ahe Macu-family believes Pitout stole the land even though he has a title deed for the farm, known as Elandsklip. Lucky Shabalala No the guy doesn’t own the farm. He doesn’t have papers that proves that he owns the farm. V/O We spoke to the Macu-family but they did not want to be interviewed on camera. However, Shabalala claims to be well acquainted with their story. Lucky Shabalala He just ploughed where the cattle of the Macu family were grazing. By force and that is where the fight started because the people said to him but you cannot plough here because our livestock are grazing here. He said but the farm belongs to me, there is nothing that you can do to me. V/O When mielie-season is over it might not be a huge problem, but when the Macu goats start eating the profits, it spells trouble. V/O Pitout maintains he did more that was required of him to accommodate the Macu’s. He fenced off 90ha of his farm for their livestock and sank a borehole for them. Anton Pitout Hulle is nie tevrede nie. Hulle wil van my ontslae raak. Hulle wil my van die plaas af hê sodat hulle kan oorneem hierso. V/O The Macu’s see it differently. They say the portion of land that they have access to is unproductive and they claim the borehole doesn’t work properly. Desperate for relief, Pitout approached the land claims court in Roodepoort. At a cost of R140 000 he was awarded an interdict, but he feels it was money wasted … Anton Pitout Land Affairs wil nie betrokke raak nie. Jy staan alleen en ek dis absoluut onregverdig en dan word jy geoormerk as rassis en hierdie verskriklike monster. LINK In South Africa, any conversation around land reform is an emotive one. One the one hand people need land, on the other there are existing landowners. Both have rights but finding a win-win solution is proving to be difficult. V/O Even the low hanging fruit of the “willing buyer, willing seller’ concept seems to be having its own problems. Elmien du Plessis The problem with a willing buyer willing seller is when the land was validated either it was not evaluated correctly by the land valuers because farmland for instance got a very specific way of valuing and then oftentimes offers were made to owners that were just so good to refuse. V/O A lot of government money was spent on purchasing land.. Elmien du Plessis Some of the land owners inflated the prices exponentially. I wouldn't say in the whole it didn't work. I still think it's a good way of acquiring land if there's cooperation. V/O Newcastle farmers Darrel Brown and Sam Nkosi, started off on the wrong foot in 1996 when Brown bought the farm where Nkosi’s family has been living since 1968. After years of disputes over land rights, something changed... Sam Nkosi I took my my own pride, I said that I’d rather sit down with Mr. Brown to tell him, “What are we fighting for? That was my biggest question. We're fighting for what? Darrel Brown When Sam and I actually started talking I agreed to cut off a piece of the farm to sell to government to sort out the problem .. V/O But this turned out to be easier said than done... Darrel Brown The frustration that we've faced is we've had no support from the Department of Land Affairs in getting the matter finalized. Sam Nkosi The government has promised us more than about seven years now waiting for the next budget that the farm should be bought. But we’re waiting for that budget for I don’t know how long now, more than seven years. V/O For Brown it is also important that Nkosi gets a formal title deed for the land once the deal is formalised. Darrel Brown Well I think everybody. Wants to feel proud 01:45 of the fact that they own something. It would give him a sense of self actualization to give him a sense of what he's achieving something and he's able and privileged to then go ahead and farm it productively and hopefully use it as a stepping stone to buy something bigger and become a proper commercial farmer. V/O In the meantime, for Brown the dark cloud of expropriation without compensation hovers on the horizon. Darrel Brown We've spent a lot of money on that land and whilst we may be willing to to sell pieces of that land or some of that land in the interests of land reform I don't think any of us want to give up our hard earned land for nothing. Elmien Du Plessis We must remember that the Constitution provides the framework so it must still be just and equitable. So if it's not just and equitable to pay nil the state will not be able to do it... V/O Du Plessis says the bill sets out examples of the types of land that could potentially be expropriated without compensation, for example abandoned or unused land. Elmien du Plessis I think what they tried to do is to just give an indication of the type of land that they have in mind just to ensure people that they don't have in mind to take big commercial working farms and to dump us into a food security crisis. PROMO 1 11” Land Reform is a complex issue, and balancing the needs of the landless with the rights of landowners is proving to be a challenge. Will the new expropriation bill be the magic bullet? PROMO 2 11” The new expropriation bill paves the way for expropriation without compensation but will it make a meaningful difference to our sluggish land reform process? PROMO 3 11” Farm dwellers with historic rights to land vs title deed owners. The precarious balancing act of Land Reform continues to be a frustration for many South Africans.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Emotions recently ran high at a meeting between Police Minister Bheki Cele, farmers, and farm dwellers in Normandien in northern KwaZulu-Natal. Cele met with the farming community over concerns about
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Farmers of all class, race and economic status claim the Dept of Land Reform is driving a wedge between South Africans in rural KZN with the tenure claim system that is not working, leaving residents with more questions than answers.
metadata.Summary: Farmers in KZN blame the department of land reform for the friction in the region. According to farmers of different races, specifically the tenure claimants are a thorn in their flesh. They also lay the spate of stock thefts and farm arson in the area at the door of these claimants. Poor policing and lack of police resources also feature. A person living on a farm can for instance claim tenancy if they can prove their family has lived on that land for longer than a certain amount of time. Yet farmers say, the department requires very little proof before they register a claim. There is also a massive disconnect between the department and SAPS with SAPS “often claiming they can’t arrest.” Ex-rugby player Anton Pitout (43) has tried to register more than ten cases against the Macu-family living on his farm Elandsklip (in the Normandien-area of Northern KZN). “I have tried opening cases for assault, intimidation and contempt of court. SAPS find a different excuse to not register the cases every time.” Of these cases, only one (for assault) is presently open. In one such case, Pitout claims he was assaulted by the Macu-family. He took a video of part of the assault. When he approached his local police, he was told they couldn’t open the case because he couldn’t prove it was him taking the video. Pitout spent R140 000 last year in order to get an interdict to stop the Macu-family chasing their goats into his crops. Since then nothing has changed. Sipho Hadebe (72) bought his farm in the same area with no government assistance. Hadebe says farmers of all races work together, but the tenant claimants and politicians “from outside” make things difficult. “Corruption has eaten all the money. Now they are coming for the farms. This government will turn Normandien into Somalia.”Abu Docrat (32) claims a local politician built a house on a part of his land and gave it to the care taker of a local school. Docrat farms cattle and sheep on just over a 1000 hectares in Normandien
metadata.Further information: Case Studies: We will interview the farmers Pitout (Afrikaans). Hadebe (isiZulu). Docrat (Indian). Somebody from land reform. Somebody from SAPS. Experts: Theo de Jager, vice chair of world agri. Elmien du Plessis, lawyer intimately involved on the government side with the land claim system. KZN Land Reform: Visual Treatment The new Land Expropriation Bill was gazetted on 9 October 2020, coupled with tensions running high about farm attacks and the lack of consistent law enforcement in our rural areas… a recipe for fear and frustration… Prof Elmien du Plessis is an expert on constitutional law and land expropriation. We meet her in a library/study setting. She will be filmed without the presenter, with 2x cameras (one sideview). She explains the new bill and the implications thereof. Link & Drone driving shots take us to KZN... The bulk of the insert will be filmed in the Normandien and Newcastle region of northern KZN. Expansive drone shots and extreme wide establishers will reveal the lush landscape to be juxtaposed against the close-ups of the destruction on the farmers’ land. Pitout’s farm shows damage from the grazing cattle and 50+ goats. Huts on the Ameen farm have been burnt down. There is also cell-phone footage of an attack on Pitout, and intimidation from the farm occupiers. The interviews with the three farmers will be filmed outside (weather permitting) in a casual stance overlooking their property, or whilst working on the farm. The plan is to let the presenter assist, hands-on, while they are doing the interview. We’re going into planting season for maize, so fields need to be ploughed etc… Pitout has a maize farm, the others have livestock incl. cattle and sheep. We will try and capture the textures of the land, with close-ups of soil, livestock, crops and whatever else we find.
